articles.title: Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg doubles down on jawing with Luka Dončić: 'He's not Michael Jordan'
articles.summary: Lendeborg conceded that he might have gone overboard with his postgame comments, but he's not budging on his on-court trash talk.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors rookie forward Yaxel Lendeborg has heard the backlash he's received from NBA fans who disagreed with him going at Los Angeles Lakers superstar guard Luka Dončić during the teams' season opener on Wednesday.

Some have harped on the viral clip of Dončić telling Lendeborg amid the 127-105 Lakers victory, "Hey, bro, you're 24 and a rookie. Relax."

Lendeborg dismissed that chatter, especially that belabored line.

"The 24-year-old rookie thing? I'm 24 in the NBA with the best job in the world," Lendeborg told reporters Friday after the Warriors' 111-108 defeat to the Memphis Grizzlies.

"Just moved my mom out to California. I'm living the dream."

Lendeborg, who starred for a national title-winning Michigan team last season after playing JUCO ball and then turning more heads at UAB , explained that he's always going to be himself because that's the way he was raised.

In that same postgame interview, he also doubled down on his jawing with Dončić.

"He's going to say what he want to say. I'm going to say what I want to say," Lendeborg noted, via ESPN's Anthony Slater . "I'm not afraid to talk to nobody, man. He's not Michael Jordan. Come on now. It's fun trash talk. I feel like I did kind of take it overboard in the media, but, I mean, it is what it is."

Dončić isn't Jordan; however, the 27-year-old Slovenian is an international icon. He's a six-time All-NBA first-teamer and a two-time league scoring champion.

That clearly doesn't faze Lendeborg, whose unfiltered commentary added to his intrigue during his meteoric rise at Michigan.

Lendeborg said he told Dončić 'he sucks'

In Wednesday's season opener, Lendeborg didn't back down from the challenge of guarding Dončić. Even though Dončić piled up 23 first-half points, only two of those came against Lendeborg, according to ESPN tracking , which had Dončić shooting 0 of 4 from the field with Lendeborg as his primary defender in the halfcourt over the opening two quarters.

Lendeborg and Dončić went back and forth throughout the contest, trading jabs amid the verbal sparring.

Notably, Lendeborg was assessed a technical foul , just before Dončić banked in a buzzer-beating prayer at the end of the first half.

After the game, Lendeborg said he told Dončić "he sucks." Lendeborg also said that he "lost all respect" for Dončić after seeing firsthand how Dončić plays.

Lendeborg put Dončić on blast for "complaining" over the course of the game. Dončić conveyed postgame that the chirping took his performance to another level.

Warriors are on board with Lendeborg's bravado

While some in the basketball world have taken issue with Lendeborg's brazen approach, he's received backing from his teammates and head coach Steve Kerr in recent days.

Kerr actually said on Thursday that he loves it.

"But Steph [Curry] had the perfect comment," Kerr said, via Luca Evans of the San Francisco Chronicle . "He loved it, too, but he said, 'Now you got to back it up.' And that's right. The way you back it up is to not get lured into that next week when we play them again or against somebody else who's doing that.

"You'd much rather rein a guy in than have to kick him in the butt. And, so, I love Yaxel's competitiveness. He's shown that he's going to be a headache for [Warriors senior vice president of communications] Raymond Ridder all year because he's willing to say anything. But I want guys to be themselves as long as they're using that wisely to help us win basketball games."

Kerr did admit, though, that Lendeborg's Wednesday night comments "became too individual."

"It's still about the team, and we got our ass kicked," Kerr said on Thursday, via Evans. "So it should be about us giving up 127 points. It doesn't matter what Luka shot against him or what the individual matchup was. We gave up 127, and we have to be better."

Draymond Green, long one of the most outspoken players in the NBA, unsurprisingly has lauded his new Warriors teammate for the way he handled the testy night against Dončić.

"I respect the hell out of Yaxel for being willing to stand toe-to-toe," Green said on his podcast this week.

"If you can't rock with a guy like that, who compete like that, who willing to fight like that, you're probably a loser. Because if you can't get behind that, all the people are going, 'Oh man, he shouldn't be talking.' Why shouldn't he? That's like this old adage of like, 'Oh, you're a rookie, you don't talk.' F*** that. Why wouldn't I talk? The guy you criticize is the guy that does that and then tuck his tail and run. That's the guy who should be criticized, not the guy who do it, stand 10 toes on it and continues to go forward."

Lendeborg offers tame remarks about latest showdown with Grizzlies' Cameron Boozer

Even though Lendeborg reinforced his stance toward Dončić on Friday, his postgame media session with reporters in the locker room showcased an additional side of the authentic, do-it-all forward.

Following his latest head-to-head with draft classmate Cameron Boozer, whom Lendeborg lost to last season while Boozer was at Duke and then beat in July to win an NBA Summer League title, Lendeborg gave credit where credit was due.

"He played a great game today," Lendeborg said of Boozer, via Slater . "We both were on the bad end with the turnovers, but we both [got our] first double-doubles. ... First career double-doubles for both of us. It was a fun matchup. Didn't really get to guard each other much. He took advantage of his matchup when I was on him. Did a great job."

Lendeborg was the 11th overall pick in this year's draft. Boozer went eight picks before him at No. 3 overall.

Lendeborg expressed after winning that Summer League championship that he thinks about revenge every time he plays Boozer. On Friday, Lendeborg maintained that he looks for an edge against his draft classmates, except he freely acknowledged that Boozer outperformed him that day.

articles.title: Valkyries Beat Dream in WNBA Finals Game 4, Box Score Stats, Highlights for Angel Reese, Top Players
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries have tied the 2026 WNBA Finals.
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries have tied the 2026 WNBA Finals.

The Vaklyries evened the series against the Atlanta Dream at 2-2 after forcing 18 turnovers in a 67-62 Game 4 road win.

Here's a look at some of the top performers and highlights from what will now be a best-of-three championship series.

Golden State shuffled its starting lineup ahead of Saturday's game by turning to Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles.

The Dream and Valkyries went on to trade buckets throughout a relatively even first quarter before the visitors went on an 18-6 run at the end of the second half.

The Valkyries went into the break holding a 16-point advantage after attempting 21 more shots over the first two frames.

That was in part because the Valkyries took advantage of struggles with ball control by the Dream, which committed 14 turnovers in the first 20 minutes.

Kiah Stokes helped the Valkyries hang onto the lead in the third quarter with a historic defensive performance.

The Dream spent the second half chipping away at the deficit, bringing the score as close as six points in the final eight minutes of the fourth.

The Valkyries held off the comeback in part thanks to a clutch three-pointer from Veronica Burton with four and a half minutes left on the clock.

The Dream pushed within four points in the final 30 seconds before the Valkyries closed out the win.

Both teams shot less than 18 percent from deep, but the Valkyries attempted more shots (72-54) and forced more turnovers (18-9).

The Dream were unable to take advantage of the Valkyries racking up fouls as the home team went 22-from-31 from the foul line.

The Valkyries opened Game 1 of the championship series with a home win before conceding consecutive losses to the Dream.

Golden State will now get the chance to retake the series lead in Game 5, which is set to tip off Monday at 8 p.m. ET in San Francisco.

articles.title: Las Valkyries asaltan Atlanta e igualan de nuevo las Finales
articles.standfirst: Nuevo partidazo de Gabby Williams con 17 puntos
articles.summary: Nuevo partidazo de Gabby Williams con 17 puntos
articles.body: Las Golden State Valkyries se impusieron a las Atlanta Dream (62-67) en el cuarto partido de las finales de la WNBA disputado este sábado, gracias a que sus estrellas Gabby Williams y Ceci Zandalasini recuperaron su mejor versión (17 y 10 puntos respectivamente) e igualan la serie por el anillo (2-2). El conjunto californiano respondió a la presión después de encadenar dos derrotas contundentes, en un encuentro en el que no dio opciones a las locales en ningún momento, quienes perdieron su primer partido en casa en los 'playoffs' esta temporada. La buena defensa de las violetas sobre Angel Reese no le permitió brillar como en los partidos anteriores y terminó con un pobre 2/12 en tiros de campo. Tras haber sufrido la peor derrota de la temporada en el tercer partido de las Finales (-26 puntos), la entrenadora Natalie Nakase introdujo dos cambios en el quinteto inicial de Golden State, en el que dio entrada al Tiff Hayes y Kaila Charles para buscar más eficacia ofensiva, dejando a la italiana Zandalasini en el banquillo. Sin embargo, la prueba no funcionó porque el comienzo siguió la tónica de los últimos duelos: sin acierto para las californianas y con las Dream lanzadas. Tras un tiempo muerto de Nakase mediado el primer tiempo, y sobre todo, con la entrada precisamente de Cecilia Zandalasini a la pista, la energía de las Valkyries cambió en defensa (con cuatro robos consecutivos y dejando a la estrella Reese en 0 puntos en el primer cuarto) y, en ataque, con un parcial de 12-0. La intensidad aumentó en un segundo período y las dos grandes estrellas de Golden State aparecieron cuando más las necesitaba su equipo. 'Ceci', con un bonita penetración por el centro sumó un 2+1, que unido a la contribución de la alero Gabby Williams (con siete puntos casi consecutivos), daban la mayor ventaja en el marcador hasta ese momento a las visitantes (+16). Atlanta recibió de su propia medicina. Es el equipo que más balones roba por partido de la liga estadounidense, pero en la primera mitad le condenaron sus 14 pérdidas. En la reanudación, las Dream se parecieron más al energético equipo que venía de sumar dos victorias seguidas para remontar la serie. Un triple lateral de la australiana Borlase recortó la distancia a solo 6 puntos (40-46). Pero las 'violetas' demostraron personalidad y contestaron cada vez que Atlanta se acercó en el luminoso para mantener la distancia. En los minutos finales, con las locales volcadas alentadas por su público, Tiff Hayes se echó a su equipo a la espalda con productivas penetraciones a canasta y un lejano tiro de tres de Burton dio aire a Golden State (55-64 a falta de 4:19 minutos). La emoción se mantuvo hasta el final. Rhyne Howard contestó con un 2+1 al 'fade-away' de Veronica Burton a falta de 28 segundos y cuatro abajo para Atlanta, pero dos triples consecutivos fallados de las locales sellaron la victoria para las Valkyries. El próximo lunes regresarán a San Francisco para el quinto partido, que se jugará en el pabellón Valhalla para desempatar unas finales que se decidirán al mejor de siete. 62 – Dream (11+15+19+17): Canada (10), Gray (5), Reese (8), Howard (19), Hillmon (6) -quinteto inicial-, Bonner (4), Borlase (10), Koné (-), Okot (-), Paopao (-) y Walker-Kimbrough (-). 67 – Valkyries (16+26+12+13): Burton (13), Williams (17), Hayes (13), Charles (5), Stokes (4) -quinteto inicial-, Thornton (3), Zandalasini (10), Gueye (-), Chen (-), Salaun (2), Amihere (-) y Jocyte (-). articles.standfirst: El partido se decidió por detalles al final
articles.summary: El partido se decidió por detalles al final
articles.body: El UCAM Murcia, con el liderazgo ofensivo de Dylan Ennis y Michael Forrest -46 puntos entre ambos-, se llevó una trabajada victoria por 88-81 ante un batallador Leyma Coruña para colocar el 2-3 en su bagaje de triunfos-derrotas tras cinco jornadas en la Liga Endesa y, aunque los universitarios aún están lejos de su mejor versión, superaron a un rival al que la buena actuación de Alonzo Verge Jr y Paul Jorgensen -25 y 20 tantos- no bastó y que continúa en zona de descenso, al ser el penúltimo con sólo un encuentro ganado. El choque se presentó con la baja de última hora en el UCAM CB del alero cubano Howard Sant-Roos por una sobrecarga articular en el tobillo derecho, la cual se unió a la arrastrada del base argentino Juani Marcos por una microrrotura fibrilar en el sóleo de la pierna izquierda. En el cuadro gallego Carles Marco dispuso de todos sus efectivos. El equipo habitualmente vestido de grana y hoy de azul arrancó con dos triples que convirtió Forrest y uno más de Kaiser Gates y una bandeja anotada por Emanuel Cate para el 11-1 inicial. Reaccionó de forma inmediata el equipo visitante de la mano de Jorgensen y un parcial de 0-11 con siete puntos del escolta neoyorquino con pasaporte italiano voltearon el resultado (11-12 en el minuto 7). Toni Nakic acabó con la sequía local desde la línea de personal y a partir de ahí Jonah Radebaugh, sumando desde la larga distancia y asistiendo para el mate de Jean-Marc Pansa, pareció aupar a los murcianos. Sin embargo, los tres últimos puntos del cuarto fueron del Leyma, que llegó a la primera pausa a un solo punto de distancia (18-17). El partido tenía más errores que aciertos -por algo ambos equipos llegaban al choque siendo el antepenúltimo y el penúltimo- y Jorgensen era el más entonado. Su segundo triple ya para 10 puntos hizo efectiva otra alternancia en el tanteador y los gallegos no se pararon ahí. Un 0-7 dejó el 18-24 y Sito Alonso lo paró desde la banda. De vuelta a la pista emergió Ennis y con el empate a 26 fue Marco el que pidió tiempo muerto. Esa tendencia se prolongó hasta el descanso. Los malos porcentajes, especialmente en los de casa, hicieron que los puntos subieran al electrónico del Palacio poco a poco. Ennis, autor de 12 al descanso, y Jorgensen, con 15, se salían de ese guion general pero los visitantes terminaron mejor y de ahí que se retiraran al vestuario tres arriba (37-40). El segundo tiempo comenzó como el primero con un triple murciano, que hizo en esta ocasión Nakic para empatar y dos tiros libres de Pansa para el 42-40. El intercambio de canastas y de fallos, demasiados, propició que ninguno de los dos equipos lograra abrir hueco. El encuentro se jugaba a tirones y así se pasó del 49-46 al 49-52 y de ahí al 58-52. El cuarto, en el que los de Sito mejoraron algo en su efectividad de lanzamiento, terminó con un resultado que auguraba emociones fuertes en los diez minutos finales. A falta de espectáculo la tensión mantenía el interés y el 63-58 dejaba el choque claramente por decidir. Un triple de Souley Boum puso una ventaja murciana que no se daba desde el arranque (66-59) pero Verge salió al rescate de su equipo respondiendo de la misma manera y también penetrando. La consecuencia de lo hecho por el base estadounidense fue que los guarismos volvieron a comprimirse. Un triple de Tomas Dimsa puso el 69-70 ya dentro de los cinco últimos minutos. También desde más allá del arco acertaron Forrest y luego Nakic cuando se encendían las alarmas para el UCAM CB. El 75-70 era oxígeno puro para los universitarios a tres minutos y 25 segundos del bocinazo. El Leyma seguía ahí y se colocó a uno con el 75-74 pero un 2+1 de Cate y luego otro de Forrest, este tras un robo de balón crucial, volvieron a establecer la diferencia en siete. Fue la sentencia definitiva. El 84-74 a 1.11 del final era el pasaporte al triunfo y así ocurrió en un duelo de alternativas en el que los locales perdieron 17 balones y su oponente 20. 88. articles.title: Angel Reese Explains Struggles After Hitting New Statistical Low in Dream's WNBA Finals G4 Loss
articles.summary: Atlanta Dream star Angel Reese reflected on her inefficient performance during the team's 67-62 loss to the Golden State Valkyries in Game 4 of the 2026 WNBA Finals.
articles.body:
Atlanta Dream star Angel Reese reflected on her inefficient performance during the team's 67-62 loss to the Golden State Valkyries in Game 4 of the 2026 WNBA Finals.

"I think I rushed a lot of my shots and I didn't take my time and finish around the basket like I've been doing in the last three games," Reese told reporters after the loss. "It happens. I'm just looking forward to the next game and I'll just be better."

While Reese excelled throughout the first three contests of the 2026 Finals, she scored just eight points while shooting 2-of-12 from the field on Saturday.

It represented her lowest field-goal percentage in any game during Atlanta's 2026 playoff run.

The series is now tied 2-2 headed into Monday night's pivotal Game 5.

It's worth noting that Reese made plays defensively on Saturday by picking up three blocks and one steal, but also committed six turnovers compared to just three assists.

Reese wasn't the only member of the Dream to struggle offensively in Game 4. Their entire lineup shot a mere 33.3 percent from the field and 17.4 percent from three. They also committed 18 turnovers.

Atlanta's 62 points were its fewest in any game throughout the team's 2026 campaign, including the playoffs.

Still, the Dream can take control of the series once again if Reese is able to look like her usual self.

The three-time All-Star has thrived throughout the playoffs, averaging 19.4 points, 10.3 rebounds, 1.8 steals and 1.8 blocks per game across eight postseason appearances heading into Saturday's action. She also connected on 48.1 percent of her field goals and 47.1 percent of her triples over that span.

Reese's productivity was a key reason why the Dream swept the Washington Mystics and New York Liberty in the first two rounds of the playoffs.

Game 5 between Atlanta and Golden State is on Monday at 8 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Angel Reese struggles badly after bold comments as Valkyries beat Dream to even WNBA Finals
articles.summary: Angel Reese's bold pregame comments backfired as she missed layup after layup in Game 4, and the Golden State Valkyries evened the WNBA Finals at 2-2.
articles.body: ATLANTA – Angel Reese said Friday that she could take Golden State’s confidence and "mess them up." On Saturday, the Valkyries made a mess of her afternoon. Reese followed two dominant performances with her worst game of the series, missing layup after layup when Atlanta needed her most. She finished with eight points and nine rebounds on 2-for-12 shooting as the Dream lost 67–62 to the Golden State Valkyries on Saturday at State Farm Arena, evening the best-of-seven WNBA Finals at 2–2. Reese also committed six turnovers. WNBA PLAYERS, COACHES REFUSE TO EXPLAIN NATIONAL ANTHEM ABSENCES AMID MOUNTING CRITICISM After combining for 51 points and 28 rebounds in Atlanta’s two victories, Reese had plenty of confidence heading into Game 4. "They’re playing into my mental game," Reese said Friday. Before tipoff, both teams again stayed off the court for the national anthem, marking their fourth straight absence in the series. They left moments before the performance and returned seconds after it ended. Once the game began, Reese struggled to finish around the basket and hold onto the ball. She went scoreless in the first quarter and reached halftime with four points, three rebounds, five turnovers and three fouls. Two of those fouls were offensive. Atlanta’s problems extended beyond Reese. The Dream committed 14 first-half turnovers and attempted just 19 shots to Golden State’s 40. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Reese’s hook shot with 6:15 left in the second quarter was Atlanta’s last field goal of the half. The Valkyries closed the period on an 18–6 run to take a 42–26 lead into the break. The Dream made a push in the third, cutting the deficit to six on Isobel Borlase’s three-pointer with 4:27 remaining. But Golden State answered with consecutive baskets from Tiffany Hayes and Gabby Williams and took a 54–45 lead into the fourth. Reese scored two points in the third, both at the foul line. Her only shot attempt was a missed three, and she picked up her fourth foul in the closing seconds. She had a chance to salvage her afternoon in the fourth quarter. Instead, she missed her first five shots of the period: three layups, a tip shot and a short hook. Atlanta got within six twice. After Veronica Burton’s three-pointer pushed Golden State’s lead to 64–55 with 4:23 remaining, Reese missed a layup, grabbed her own rebound and missed the tip. On Atlanta’s next possession, she missed a 5-foot hook. The Dream needed their star to deliver. She kept leaving points at the rim. Reese finally made a driving layup with 1:36 remaining, her first field goal since the second quarter, cutting the deficit to 64–59. Before that basket, she had missed six layups, including one blocked by Kiah Stokes. Atlanta still had a chance. But Allisha Gray and Borlase missed threes on the same possession, and Burton’s jumper with 34.6 seconds left stretched the lead back to seven. Rhyne Howard’s three-point play brought Atlanta within four with 28.7 seconds remaining. Burton made one of two free throws, and the Dream’s final possession ended with another Reese mistake. She grabbed two offensive rebounds to keep it alive, then threw a pass that Williams stole with 9.8 seconds left. It was her sixth turnover. articles.body: Even though former quarterback Brendan Sorsby was obviously not on the field today for No. 8 Texas Tech, the Cincinnati Bearcats had this game circled on the calendar for nearly an entire year. Call it a revenge game for what had taken place leading up to the 2026 season, or the Red Raiders finally running into a team that could present a viable challenge, this expensive roster that was assembled through the transfer portal ran into a buzz saw on Saturday afternoon. Cincinnati would end up winning 37-24, in a game that never truly felt close after the opening 10 minutes. But most importantly, the Red Raiders are just not as explosive as what we saw in 2025. For a lot of college football fans, they will look at this result as karma for making their Big 12 colleagues file a federal lawsuit in order to scare Texas Tech enough to end the charade surrounding Sorsby suiting up for the Red Raiders this season. articles.title: Núñez firma su mejor partido en Liga Endesa para tumbar al Zaragoza
articles.standfirst: El madrileño brilla junto a Nkamhoua y Minaya
articles.summary: El madrileño brilla junto a Nkamhoua y Minaya
articles.body: El Barcelona encontró un líder inesperado ante el Casademont Zaragoza. Tras un mal partido ante el Joventut que confirmaba un complicado arranque de temporada, Juan Núñez firmó su mejor partido anotador en la Liga Endesa para tumbar al equipo maño 99-81. Núñez no ha contado con la confianza de Sekulic, pero el esloveno se tuvo que rendir al madrileño tras ver lo que era capaz ante el Zaragoza. Núñez firmó 23 puntos, tope de su carrera en la Liga Endesa, con 7/9 en tiros de dos y 2/2 en triples, y acabó con 22 de valoración, también tope personal, sin dar una sola asistencia, eso sí. El base fue el jugador que mantuvo a flote al Barça cuando el Casademont Zaragoza más apretó, en el primer tiempo. Ahí dio un recital y castigó la elección de la defensa maña de flotarle en los tiros. Luego, en la segunda parte lo remató a la sombra de Olivier Nkamhoua y Justin Minaya. En el primer acto el Zaragoza recibió el palo de la lesión de Homesley que se retiró tras caer mal al aterrizar después de poner un tapón, y ya no volvió. El Barça estableció ligeras ventajas en el primer cuatro, 24-21, y al descanso, 48-40, pero fue su salida en el tercer acto lo que decantó el partido. Un parcial de 14-0, en el que contribuyeron los tres protagonistas del choque, dejó casi sentenciado el partido (62-40) al final del ese periodo tan decisivo hubo una pequeña reacción maña (0-5) que dejó el 72-57 en el marcador. Esa reacción tuvo continuidad en el cuarto periodo con un 2-12 de parcial (2-17 con los cinco puntos del tercer cuarto), para congelar el Palau, 74-69. Pero de nuevo los triples de Nkamhoua y Minaya dispararon al Barça que en poco tiempo estaba en un cclaro 87-73 y que acabó con el 99-81 definitivo. El impacto de Nkamhoua y Minaya se puede apreciar en el +/- de ambos en el partido. El francés acabó con un impresionante +36 mientras que el estadounidense logró un +28. Núñez fue el mejor anotador del Barça con esos 23 puntos, Nkamhoua y Brizuela hicieron 14 y Nebo acabó con 12. En el Zaragoza Olaseni firmó 18 y Brussino 15. Vives por su parte sigue a un nivel que tendrá que hacer pensar a Chus Mateo si no cuenta con él para las próximas Ventanas de clasificación.

articles.title: Vidorreta se reivindica: "Parece que se me ha olvidado el baloncesto desde que llegué a Málaga"
articles.standfirst: El técnico, algo molesto por cómo se ve al club en los medios y la afición
articles.summary: El técnico, algo molesto por cómo se ve al club en los medios y la afición
articles.body: Txus Vidorreta alzó la voz. El entrenador del Unicaja mostró este viernes en la sala de prensa del Martín Carpena un tono especialmente reivindicativo para defender el trabajo que está realizando el equipo y, de paso, reivindicar su propia trayectoria. El técnico cajista considera que tanto los resultados como el juego del conjunto malagueño están siendo infravalorados y puso varios datos sobre la mesa para respaldar su discurso. El entrenador del Unicaja no quiso esconder su malestar. "¿Cómo no voy a estar reivindicativo si hemos ganado en una cancha muy complicada por doce puntos de diferencia?", señaló en referencia al triunfo en Manresa. Vidorreta recordó que esa victoria, por la diferencia obtenida, es la más amplia lograda por un equipo en Liga Regular en esa pista en prácticamente la última década. El técnico también puso en contexto aquel resultado. Manresa, pese a las bajas de Colenda, Allen y Villar, fue capaz de anotar 108 puntos tres días después ante la Roma. El Unicaja, por su parte, también afrontó aquel encuentro con tres ausencias. Para Vidorreta, el triunfo cajista tuvo mucho más valor del que se le concedió. "Parece que no sirve de nada que haya sido tres veces semifinalista en los últimos seis años de la competición, porque se me ha olvidado todo desde que he llegado a Málaga. Parece que no sé nada de baloncesto", afirmó con contundencia. El entrenador bilbaíno quiso respaldar su reivindicación con números y recordó su trayectoria reciente: presencia en Final Four de la Basketball Champions League, semifinales y finales de Copa y dos semifinales consecutivas de la Liga Endesa. "Voy a reivindicarme un poco porque esos son datos. Voy a hablar solo de datos", insistió. Y también defendió el rendimiento de su actual equipo: "Los datos del equipo son buenos, porque compite, defiende, juega como tal y lleva cuatro victorias consecutivas". Vidorreta amplió su defensa al trabajo del director deportivo, Juanma Rodríguez. "No va por alguien en concreto. Es una generalización. Es lo que se percibe en general. Cualquier mensaje que lanzamos Juanma o yo no sirve de nada", explicó. El técnico también quiso reivindicar la manera de jugar del Unicaja. Especialmente satisfecho se mostró con la actuación del equipo en Pardubice, pese al escaso acierto exterior. "Llamó poderosamente la atención lo bien que jugamos al baloncesto en Pardubice, a nivel europeo. Qué manera de compartir la pelota, qué número de pases y qué cantidad de tiros liberados. Lo que pasa es que, si haces diez de 35, es muy difícil brillar", analizó.

articles.title: Golden State Valkyries beat Atlanta Dream 67-62 to even the WNBA Finals at 2-2
articles.summary: Gabby Williams scored 17 points and led a stellar defensive effort to beat the Atlanta Dream 67-62 on Saturday and even the WNBA Finals 2-2.
articles.body: ATLANTA — Gabby Williams gave a passionate speech to her teammates after Golden State fell behind in the WNBA Finals, saying she had to show a “different type of fire." The Valkyries leader did just that as she scored 17 points and led a stellar defensive effort to beat the Atlanta Dream 67-62 on Saturday and even the WNBA Finals 2-2. “I didn’t like my last game. I didn’t like who I was in that last game,” Williams said. “So I think stepping up in that role made me step up also individually. If I want to lead my team, I have to be the one that sets the tone and I have to lead by example, as well. So I think that motivated me to set the tempo today.” Tiffany Hayes was moved into the starting lineup and scored all of her 13 points in the second half, while Kiah Stokes anchored the defensive effort that stymied Angel Reese, who had double-doubles in the first three games. Golden State will host Game 5 of the best-of-seven series Monday. Stokes, who won three WNBA championships while playing with Las Vegas, grabbed 16 rebounds, including eight on the offensive end. After Atlanta rolled to a 97-71 victory in Game 3, she told the Valkyries they only needed to worry about winning the next game. “One thing that I had told the team after the last game is the goal when we play on the road ... just steal one on the road. So yeah, we lost on Wednesday. But to me, that doesn’t mean we’re out of anything,” Stokes said, “because our goal was there and could still be accomplished if we won today, and then we go back home.” “Now it’s the best-of-three series," Stokes added. "So it was just shake it off and learn from it and then just get ready. Nothing was won or lost in Game 3.” Reese, like the rest of her teammates, struggled on offense. Reese had just eight points and nine rebounds after dominating the previous two games while averaging 25.5 points and 14 rebounds in the Dream victories. Reese missed 10 of her 12 shots, including a few layups in the fourth quarter. “I think it was me. I think I rushed a lot on my shots and I didn’t take my time and finish around the basket like I’ve been doing the last three games,” Reese said. “It happens and I’m just looking forward to the next game and just do it.” Atlanta shot 33.3% overall and only 4 for 23 from 3-point range. Rhyne Howard finished with 19 points to lead the Dream. Even as poorly as they played at times, the Dream trimmed a 16-point halftime deficit to 61-55 midway through the fourth quarter, bringing fans in the sellout crowd of over 17,000 to their feet. Golden State answered with a 3-pointer by Veronica Burton to briefly silence them. The Dream then scored seven of the next nine points, including a three-point play by Howard with 28 seconds left to get within 66-62. Burton then made the first of two free throws a second later and Atlanta couldn’t convert on the other end as once again Golden State challenged shots led by Stokes. She finished with three blocks and now has a WNBA Finals record of 14 in the four games, surpassing the old record of 12 by Brittney Griner and Sylvia Fowles. “I just hang my head on defense. I like to block shots,” Stokes said. Coach Natalie Nakase also made a change in the starting lineup, Hayes and Kaila Charles for Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini. While the Valkyries got off to a slow start again in the early afternoon tipoff with the Atlanta Hawks playing their home opener at night, when Thornton and Zandalasini entered the game they paid immediate dividends. The two helped a key first-quarter run that gave Golden State its first lead since the third quarter of Game 2. Atlanta got within 24-20 on Reese’s basket — her lone one of the first half — but the Valkyries responded with an 18-6 run to close the half. The 42-26 deficit at the break was the largest that the Dream had faced all playoffs. Atlanta had dominated the third quarter in the WNBA Finals, outscoring Golden State 60-35 in the first three games. Atlanta managed just a 19-12 edge in Game 4.

articles.title: After two rough endings, why Wemby and the Spurs are a long way from panic
articles.summary: Wembanyama and company already proved last season that experience is overrated. Now, in a different way, they have to do it again.
articles.body:
AUSTIN - Victor Wembanyama couldn't quite make it around an Amen corner Friday night. But even his dejection came with a bright side.

In the NBA, as at Augusta National, people really don't start to care if you can navigate the toughest hazards until the spring.

The next time Wembanyama takes aim at Houston's pine tree on a pogo stick, he will do so with a little more course knowledge, as well as a better approach. In April or May, if the Rockets again put Amen Thompson on him with a game on the line, he might try what he wished he'd attempted in the closing seconds of a 114-110 Spurs loss at Moody Center.

"I would've dunked the ball," Wembanyama said.

Maybe Thompson will have something to say about that the next time, just as he did Friday with a right-handed swat of Wembanyama's left-handed layup. The 6-foot-7 forward went three picks after the 7-4 center in the 2023 draft, but he's not exactly intimidated by the disparity in height or hype.

"I can jump pretty high," Thompson told reporters after the game . "I wouldn't try to keep ducking (in on) me, but you know, if they want to, they can."

That's the kind of early-season bravado the Spurs oozed a year ago, when they were the young guys piling up highlights and victories against established contenders with targets on their backs. Back then, some of those established contenders assumed they were good enough to turn things on when it mattered.

But that assumption was a mistake. And now the Spurs have to avoid making the same one.

As guard De'Aaron Fox put it standing in the middle of a borrowed University of Texas home locker room Friday night, the Spurs "can't just expect to flip a switch when the games start counting."

Even though their two opening-week losses came against probably the two best non-San Antonio teams in the Western Conference, the current version of the Spurs is not even close to what they expect from themselves, and Fox noted there's probably a reason for that.

"Our preseason was (poopy)," Fox said, using a less family-friendly term for that sentiment.

And really, it was easy to see all of this coming. Say what you will about how these guys are highly paid professionals, and about how it's their job to treat exhibition dates against Atlanta and Phoenix like they're the most important thing in the world, you don't need to consult UT's newly renowned fourth-and-2 data analytics platform to explain why that didn't happen.

Of course a group of guys who just played in the NBA Finals four months ago were going to be challenged to approach October with the same winner-take-all urgency. And of course good teams like the Thunder and Rockets, who both entered this season with things to prove against the reigning conference champs, would be ready to pounce on every Spurs misstep.

An 0-2 start isn't reason for anything in the same stratosphere as panic, and it's not even unique among teams that played for a league championship last June. The New York Knicks, you might have noticed, also dropped their first two games of the season, and the Spurs have at least a couple of reasons to think their return to action has been a little better than that.

For one, no San Antonio player has had to publicly express his disappointment with the franchise the way extension-seeking Knicks star Karl-Anthony Towns has .

For another, Spurs' ownership thus far has not been reported to have used the success of last season to rope team employees into more cybersecurity training, the way James Dolan's Knicks reportedly did with a championship ring phishing email .

So far, at least, the vibes around the Spurs remain rightfully and overwhelmingly positive, and that was evident even when coach Mitch Johnson and his players couldn't help chuckling at the inevitable questions Friday about whether there's reason for "concern."

"How many games are left?" Dylan Harper asked, knowing that the answer lands somewhere between 80 and 108.

Obviously, that doesn't mean the first two don't count. And obviously, that doesn't mean the little hiccups accompanying the team's increasing usage of a Harper-Fox-Stephon Castle lineup are guaranteed to work themselves out.

Adjustments will be necessary. That's true of not only the three point guards, but also of everybody on the roster.

It isn't supposed to look now like it's supposed to look in the spring. Gregg Popovich's teams, the best of which built toward a post-rodeo peak, always understood that.

But those teams also didn't take progress for granted. In the fall of 2013, the last time the Spurs were coming off an NBA Finals heartbreak, they knew that what mattered most was what happened the following June.

But even with that knowledge? Those Spurs still started the regular season 13-1, and remained relentless all the way through their championship redemption tour.

This time, it probably won't go as smoothly. This version of the Spurs hasn't been together as long. And just as some worried last season about whether they had enough experience to make it through the playoffs, having never done it before? The same question can be asked about whether they know enough to handle a Finals hangover.

Wembanyama and company already proved once that experience is overrated. Now, in a different way, they have to do it again.

And if that process takes him back to basketball's Amen corner?

At least now he knows which shot not to try.

articles.title: Is Suns big Drew Timme failing to pass the eye test in NBA?
articles.summary: The Phoenix Suns' big Drew Timme has joined the team on a two-way deal.
articles.body:
Phoenix Suns forward Drew Timme didn't sugarcoat why he's with his sixth NBA team in three seasons and has yet to fully establish himself in the league.

"I mean, honestly, I'm an undersized white guy," he said after morning shootaround at the team's practice facility on Oct. 24.

"I don't pass the eye test, I would say, but I know how to hoop and play and make people better, and I think that's a skill that's undervalued and something that maybe doesn't always show up in the stats sheet, but something that's impactful and you really have to be around to see it. Just finding where you fit because I'm not going to fit every style of play."

Phoenix claimed the 6-9, 235-pound Timme off waivers after the Minnesota Timberwolves let him go heading into the 2026-27 season.

Timme is on a two-way deal with the Suns.

"I love their style of play," Timme said about the Suns. "Just their movement. The coaches have been great. The trust that they give the players from what I've seen and stuff. It's a great spot. It's a team that wants to win and needs to win. I just want to be able to help them in any way possible."

With Oso Ighodaro sidelined (right oblique strain) and Mark Williams (left shoulder surgery) expected to miss multiple months, Phoenix lacks its normal depth at the big position.

Suns coach Jordan Ott is viewing Ighodaro's injury as a "day-to-day." Playing every game last season, Ighodaro suffered his injury late in the first half of the 41-point road loss to the Portland Trail Blazers in the season opener for both teams.

Khaman Maluach starts at center, two-way player Duop Reath is his backup, but the physical and versatile Timme can play both the four and five.

"I can kind of just be a plug-and-play kind of guy," Timme said. "I've been around the league a little bit and stuff and pretty experienced. So, kind of just filling any gap that needs to be filled. Any role I can, whether it's a four, five, maybe a little pressure release and stuff like that, be a connector. So just kind of anything in that role."

Timme, 26, played nine games (two starts) with the Brooklyn Nets in the 2024-25 season and averaged 12.1 points and 7.2 rebounds.

He joined the Los Angeles Lakers last season on a two-way contract. He saw action in 27 games, starting one, and averaged 3.4 points.

Before his stint with Brooklyn, Timme was on Exhibit 10 deals with the Milwaukee Bucks in 2023 and the Sacramento Kings in 2024, but he was waived by both teams.

Now Timme is with Phoenix, his sixth NBA team.

"I feel like I'm in a great spot," Timme said. "College was great, great time, and then my first (year in NBA), came in, learning the ropes, changing the game a little bit, and now I've shot, not on high attempts, but I shot pretty good last year. Just trying to continue to build on that, the confidence, the reps and the growth in that, especially my shooting. I think that's something that could really help kind of establish myself more in this league."

Timme shot 44% from 3 (11-of-25) from distance last season with the Lakers.

"Also just being an everyday guy, and like I said, being a guy that can fix any problem, or kind of just plug and play anywhere," Timme continued. "I think that's something that really can help establish myself."

With every stint, Timme believes he learned a great deal that's factored in receiving opportunities with different NBA teams.

"Just watching from guys that have been in the league and seeing their habits and stuff," Timme said. "Obviously, you got guys like Book (Devin Booker) and even like Luke (Kennard), who I was with last year. Just seeing how their daily habits and how they approached the game, it's great to learn from."

Timme and Luke Kennard were teammates last season with the Lakers.

"When you're a guy who's on the fringe and like really trying to establish himself, it's like, it's watching guys like that," Timme said. "Whether I was watching Bron (LeBron James) last year (with the Lakers). Try to be as good of a learner as you can."

Timme shouted out Ighodaro for helping him with adjusting to his new team.

"Oso has been great," Timme said. "I've only been here two or three days, and he's just been in my ear constantly helping me with the plays, the terminology and stuff. It's great because it's tough coming to do a new spot just quickly and already in season and stuff, because I didn't get training camp with (the Suns). He's been great, especially another front court guy. It's great."

From Richardson, Texas, Timme (pronounced TIM-ee) was a three-time All-American at Gonzaga, where he became the school's all-time leading scorer with 2,307 points in four years, but he went undrafted in 2023

He spent three seasons in the G League, averaging 15.9 points on 56% shooting and 6.9 rebounds in 48 career games.
